chapters.title: And He Called
chapters.html:
Leviticus 1

From the Herd

1And He called to Moses, and the LORD spoke to him from the tent of meeting, saying,

2"Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When any of you brings an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering from the livestock — from the herd or from the flock.

3If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall bring an unblemished male. He shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of meeting, for his acceptance before the LORD.

4And he shall lean his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it will be accepted for him, to make atonement for him.

5And he shall slaughter the young bull before the LORD, and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall bring the blood and dash the blood against the altar all around, the altar at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

6And he shall skin the burnt offering and cut it into its pieces.

7And the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire on the altar and lay out wood on the fire.

8And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall lay out the pieces, the head and the suet, on the wood that is on the fire that is on the altar.

9And its entrails and its legs he shall wash with water, and the priest shall turn all of it into smoke on the altar — a burnt offering, an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

From the Flock

10And if his offering is from the flock, from the sheep or from the goats, for a burnt offering, he shall bring an unblemished male.

11And he shall slaughter it on the north flank of the altar before the LORD, and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall dash its blood against the altar all around.

12And he shall cut it into its pieces, with its head and its suet, and the priest shall lay them out on the wood that is on the fire that is on the altar.

13And the entrails and the legs he shall wash with water, and the priest shall bring all of it and turn it into smoke on the altar. It is a burnt offering, an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

From the Birds

14And if his offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, he shall bring his offering from the turtledoves or from the young pigeons.

15And the priest shall bring it to the altar and pinch off its head and turn it into smoke on the altar, and its blood shall be drained out against the wall of the altar.

16And he shall remove its crop with its feathers and throw it beside the altar, on the east side, at the place of the ashes.

17And he shall tear it open by its wings without severing it, and the priest shall turn it into smoke on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. It is a burnt offering, an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

Notes

  • v1 "And He called" — va-yiqra, a verb with no subject named, and it is the first word of the book. Hebrew tradition titles books by their opening words, so this book is simply called Vayiqra, And He Called. The English name comes from the Greek by way of the Latin and means about the Levites, which is a description of the contents; the Hebrew name is the first thing that happens in it.

  • v1 and it answers the last verse of Exodus — Exodus closed with Moses could not come into the tent of meeting, because the cloud had settled on it (40:35). The man who built the tent was shut out of it. The next sentence in the Bible is this one: he is called, and the voice comes to him from the tent of meeting. The problem at the end of one book is solved in the first four words of the next, and neither book says so.

  • v2 "when any of you" — adam ki yaqriv mikkem, and adam is the word from the first chapters of Genesis: the human being, the one made from adamah, the ground. Hebrew has ish for a man and could have used it. The sacrificial law opens by addressing the species.

  • v2 "offering" — qorban, from qarav, to come near. The causative hiqriv — used four times in this chapter — means to bring something near. A sacrifice in Hebrew is not named for what happens to it; it is named for what it is for. It is the thing you bring near with, because you cannot go near yourself.

  • v3 "burnt offering" — olah, from alah, to go up. Not named for burning but for rising: the whole animal goes up in smoke and nothing comes back down to the table. It is the only offering in the system where the worshipper eats none of it.

  • v3 "for his acceptance before the LORD" — li-rtsono, and the pronoun is not fixed. It can mean for his acceptance — so that God will receive him — or of his own will, voluntarily. Hebrew grammar allows either and the verse does not choose. Both readings are about the same question: whose willingness is at stake.

  • v4 "he shall lean his hand" — ve-samakh yado, and samakh is not a touch. It is the verb for putting weight on a thing: leaning on a wall, propping something up. The hand does not rest on the head, it presses.

  • v5 who does the killing — the verbs in vv3–6 have one subject, the man who brought the animal: he shall bring, he shall lean his hand, he shall slaughter, he shall skin it, he shall cut it into its pieces. The priests take over only at the blood. An Israelite with a bull at the tent door cuts its throat himself, in front of everyone, and then butchers it. Nothing in the chapter is done on his behalf until the blood is in a bowl.

  • v9 "a soothing aroma" — reiach nichoach, from nuach, to rest, to settle. The first time this phrase occurs in the Bible is Genesis 8:21, when Noah comes out of the ark and burns offerings, and God smells it and resolves never again to curse the ground. The man's name, Noach, is built from the same three letters — though Genesis 5:29 explains it from a different root, nacham, to comfort. The smell is one that settles: it is not a fragrance, it is a subsiding.

  • v11 "the north flank of the altar" — yerekh ha-mizbeach, the thigh of the altar, the same noun that is the hip joint at Genesis 32:25 and the side of the dwelling at Exodus 40:22. Hebrew gives built things bodies as a matter of course.

  • v15 "pinch off its head" — malaq, a verb that occurs twice in the Hebrew Bible, here and at 5:8, and both times of a bird's neck. 5:8 adds the detail that fixes it: at the back of its neck, and he shall not sever it. The head is opened from the bird, not taken off it. This whole section is the poor man's version of the same rite — a bird instead of a bull — and it is given the same closing sentence, word for word, as the bull in v9.

chapters.title: The Offering Without Blood
chapters.html:
Leviticus 2

Flour, Oil, Frankincense

1And when a person brings an offering of a grain offering to the LORD, his offering shall be fine flour, and he shall pour oil on it and put frankincense on it.

2And he shall bring it to Aaron's sons, the priests, and one shall scoop out from it his handful of its fine flour and of its oil, with all its frankincense, and the priest shall turn its memorial portion into smoke on the altar — an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

3And what is left of the grain offering shall be Aaron's and his sons' — most holy, from the offerings by fire of the LORD.

Baked, Griddled, Panned

4And when you bring an offering of a grain offering baked in an oven, it shall be unleavened loaves of fine flour mixed with oil, or unleavened wafers spread with oil.

5And if your offering is a grain offering on a griddle, it shall be fine flour mixed with oil, unleavened.

6Break it into pieces and pour oil on it. It is a grain offering.

7And if your offering is a grain offering in a pan, it shall be made of fine flour with oil.

8And you shall bring the grain offering that is made from these to the LORD, and present it to the priest, and he shall bring it near to the altar.

9And the priest shall lift up from the grain offering its memorial portion and turn it into smoke on the altar — an offering by fire, a soothing aroma to the LORD.

10And what is left of the grain offering shall be Aaron's and his sons' — most holy, from the offerings by fire of the LORD.

What May Not Go Up, and What Must

11No grain offering that you bring to the LORD shall be made with leaven, for you shall not turn any sourdough or any honey into smoke as an offering by fire to the LORD.

12As an offering of firstfruits you may bring them to the LORD, but they shall not go up on the altar for a soothing aroma.

13And every offering of your grain offering you shall salt with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant of your God be missing from your grain offering. With all your offerings you shall bring salt.

14And if you bring a grain offering of firstfruits to the LORD, you shall bring fresh ears roasted in fire, crushed grain of the fresh ear, as your grain offering of firstfruits.

15And you shall put oil on it and lay frankincense on it. It is a grain offering.

16And the priest shall turn its memorial portion into smoke — from its crushed grain and from its oil, with all its frankincense — an offering by fire to the LORD.

Notes

  • v1 "grain offering" — minchah, and the word has nothing to do with grain. It means a gift, and specifically the kind of gift that acknowledges a difference in rank: what a subject sends a king, what Jacob sends ahead to Esau. The first two occurrences in the Bible are Genesis 4:3–5, where Cain brings a minchah of the fruit of the ground and Abel brings one from his flock — the same noun covers both, and it is the word the whole quarrel turns on. By the time it reaches this chapter it has narrowed to the bloodless offering, but it still means tribute.

  • v1 "a person" — nefesh, where 1:2 had adam. Nefesh is the breath, the life, the throat — the word rendered soul in most English Bibles and never meaning a spirit separable from a body. The animal chapter addresses the human being; the flour chapter addresses the appetite.

  • v2 "its memorial portion" — azkarah, from zakhar, to remember, and the noun occurs only in the sacrificial laws. It is the handful that goes into the fire while the rest goes to the priests, and the name does not say whose memory it serves. Either God is being reminded of the giver, or the giver is reminding himself. The word is built so that both fit, and nothing in the law decides it.

  • v3 "most holy" — qodesh qadashim, holiness of holinesses, the same construction applied to the altar at Exodus 40:10 and the name of the inner room. It is said here of a priest's dinner. The leftovers of a bag of flour carry the highest grade of holiness the system has.

  • v6 "Break it into pieces" — patot otah pittim, literally crumble it crumbs: the verb takes its own noun, which is how Hebrew presses a word and how English only stutters. The noun pat survives as the ordinary word for a morsel of bread — a pat of bread is what Abraham offers the three men at Genesis 18:5.

  • v11 "no leaven… and no honey" — two things banned from the fire, and neither is explained. Both are agents of fermentation; both make dough rise and go sour on their own. Devash covers bee honey and thick fruit syrup alike. What the verse forbids is not sweetness or sourness but what they do — the altar takes nothing that changes by itself.

  • v12 what is brought but not burned — the same leaven and honey may be presented as an offering of firstfruits; they simply do not go up on the altar. Two verses, and the distinction they draw is one an English reader can miss entirely: a thing can be given to the LORD and still be wrong to burn.

  • v13 "the salt of the covenant of your God" — stated three times in one verse, from three directions: salt your offering, do not let the salt be missing, bring salt with everything. No reason is given and no story is attached. Salt is the preservative that stops exactly what leaven and honey start, which sets the verse directly against v11 — but the text calls it a covenant rather than a preservative, and leaves the phrase standing with no explanation anywhere in the Torah.

  • v14 "fresh ears roasted in fire" — aviv, the barley at the green stage, before it hardens. It is also a month: the month of Aviv, the one Israel left Egypt in (Exodus 34:18), named for the condition of the grain when the year turns. So the firstfruits offering here and the calendar itself are named by the same word, and the month is measured by a crop rather than by a number.
